The mechanism

Build an exact arithmetic selector

Turn a test for primality into arithmetic that selects the first prime above a bound. Factorial congruences, greatest common divisors, and valuations organise the selection. The construction is useful here because each stage has an exact role in isolating the answer.

What becomes elementary: The desired selection is expressed by a finite formula, with its correctness separated from questions of computational efficiency.

Track what each arithmetic test retains. The study is an exact construction; it does not claim a practical improvement over prime-search algorithms.

Explore further constructions. Edition dates, sources and reference chapters identify the scope of each study.

Introduction

This problem was mentioned to me on IRC. The following argument explains why the construction works: one stage isolates a finite set of primes, and the other uses factorial valuations to distinguish its smallest member.

There are two separate filters in the formula. The first filter is

The factor prevents primes larger than from appearing, while the congruence condition modulo prevents primes at most from appearing. What remains is precisely the set of primes strictly between and .

The second filter is more subtle. Once has been shown to be a squarefree product

the number gives each prime factor the same exponent . Dividing by subtracts the exponent with which appears in . Smaller primes appear more often in , so the smallest prime is the one whose exponent is reduced the most. The definition of then removes the common remaining power of , and the final gcd detects which primes are still present. Exactly one prime has disappeared: .
